claims.text: High configurational entropy favors a homogeneous solid solution in high-entropy nanoparticles.
Thermally activated, element-specific diffusion competes with configurational-entropy stabilization.
Atomic-size mismatch produces lattice strain that drives or facilitates diffusion.
When diffusion barriers remain high, the nanoparticles retain a single-phase solid-solution structure.
When diffusion barriers are overcome at high temperatures, elemental segregation and phase separation occur.
The target initial state is a homogeneous solid-solution nanoparticle containing at least five metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The proposed thermal exposure spans 473–1923 K.
Lattice strain arising from atomic-size mismatch affects diffusion activation energies during high-temperature exposure.
At low temperatures, configurational entropy stabilizes the solid solution.
A sufficiently large atomic-size mismatch lowers diffusion barriers.
Lower diffusion barriers permit element-specific mobility that causes local segregation and phase separation as temperature increases.
Nanoparticles with lower lattice strain preserve a homogeneous structure at elevated temperatures.
Minimal-strain nanoparticles will retain a single-phase homogeneous structure throughout 473–1923 K.
Minimal-strain nanoparticles will retain stable catalytic and thermoelectric properties throughout 473–1923 K.
Higher-strain nanoparticles will exhibit elemental segregation and possible phase separation at higher temperatures.
Segregation or phase separation in higher-strain nanoparticles will degrade catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
The prediction is scoped to controlled inert atmospheres and uniform heating rates.
Oxidative atmospheres or synthesis variations may alter diffusion behavior and stability.
